transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-18
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (QuantumEdge CTO), Samir Patel (QuantumEdge ML Eng), Laura Kim (QuantumEdge Infra)

--- Auto-generated summary (may be rough) ---
Purpose: Scope POC for latency/throughput SLOs and measurement plan; define success criteria and timelines.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um quick intros, i'm maya from redwood, ace for this region, and diego from our se team is with me.
[00:07] Priya: hey thanks, priya here, samir and laura are with me i think you have our roster.
[00:12] Diego: yep thanks, excited to dig in. high level, we want to nail down TTFT vs TPOT definitions and concrete p95/p99 targets that align with your UX.
[00:22] Samir: yeah, that'd be great. our main blocker is unpredictable tail latency during peak spikes. we run a lot of interactive use cases, so time to first token matters for perceived latency.
[00:33] Laura: and infra wants to understand throughput and how many pods/gpus we need for our committed qps.
[00:38] Maya: perfect, so quick clarification on terminology  we use TTFT for time-to-first-token (time from request arrival to first generated token) and TPOT for time-per-token (avg time to generate each subsequent token). both are important: TTFT impacts initial UX, TPOT impacts sustained streaming performance and cost.
[00:51] Priya: ok makes sense. can you propose targets?
[00:54] Diego: sure  from similar deployments we recommend starting with TTFT p95 < 180ms, p99 < 320ms for small/medium models on dedicated hardware, and TPOT p95 ~ 9ms/token, p99 < 25ms/token when working with typical generation lengths. these are baseline targets, we can adjust by model size and sequence length.
[01:15] Priya: wow p95 180ms seems tight. our current provider is more like p95 400ms on average. is that for H100 or A100?
[01:24] Diego: that's for optimized stacks on H100-class. on A100 you'd expect slightly higher numbers, and if you have cold KV cash  sorry KV cache  cold starts will add. we should run both cold and warm-cache tests.
[01:34] Maya: also wanted to call out TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs: batching increases throughput but hurts TTFT, so we need to define acceptable batching windows for your app.
[01:43] Samir: our user flows are short prompts + 256 token answers, typical qps per user is low but concurrent users at peak hit 600 qps aggregate.
[01:51] Laura: our infra constraint: we have up to 8 GPUs available for the pilot, want to see if that hits your throughput SLOs.
[01:58] Diego: good context. for workload sizing we'll need your traffic histogram: request size distribution, sequence length distribution, and concurrency spikes. Priya, can you share that?
[02:07] Priya: yes we'll export a 7 day sample  should be able to share by monday.
[02:11] Maya: excellent. on the benchmark plan: we'll do microbenchmarks (single-stream for TTFT, open-loop to measure TPOT and throughput, closed-loop to estimate end-to-end qps under realistic client pacing). we also recommend a production-replay run against a staging endpoint.
[02:26] Samir: what sample sizes do you need to get meaningful p99 numbers?
[02:29] Diego: aim for at least 1,000 end-to-end samples per test condition; for p99 confidence we prefer 5-10k where possible, and run separate tests for cold vs warm KV cache, and for different batch target sizes (no-batch, small-batch, large-batch).
[02:44] Priya: ok. how do you measure TPOT for streaming  is it per-token time or throughput measures?
[02:48] Diego: both. we capture per-token latencies on the worker side and also compute tokens/sec aggregate. TPOT reported as ms/token at p50/p95/p99 is useful, and tokens/sec at the cluster level for capacity planning.
[02:58] Maya: example success criteria we suggest: TTFT p95 < 180ms, p99 < 320ms; TPOT p95 <= 12ms/token for seq_len 256, and sustained cluster throughput to support 600 qps with <10% CPU/GPU scheduler overhead. plus quality regression checks  generation quality must not drop >2% on your eval set.
[03:18] Laura: that quality check is new to our infra rubric but makes sense. how do you validate quality?
[03:22] Diego: we run a small eval harness with your prompt set and compute automated metrics plus a manual sanity sample. we'll include eval scripts in the repo.
[03:31] Priya: timeline question  how long until we can see baseline numbers?
[03:35] Maya: once we get your traffic profile and selection of a model variant, we can run a baseline microbench within 3 business days; then schedule a production replay/staging run which typically takes 1 week to coordinate. so target review the week of Mar 25.
[03:49] Samir: model variants  what do you recommend for our use case?
[03:52] Diego: start with a medium-size open model (like our curated M variant) to validate latency; if results are good and accuracy acceptable, test a larger L variant for quality comparison. we also provide quantized runtime profiles  4-bit may reduce TPOT but we need to run regen quality checks.
[04:06] Priya: ok, and on security/compliance  we need SOC2 type2 evidence and KMS integration for keys.
[04:12] Maya: we'll share security pack and SOC2 report; Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and VPC peering for the pilot. we'll attach docs in the follow up email.
[04:21] Laura: network-wise, what's the expected egress for the pilot? we have bandwidth caps in our colo.
[04:25] Diego: estimation depends on average response size; for 256 tokens avg response ~ 2-3 KB per response compressed, at 600 qps that's about ~5 MB/s peak, plus overhead. we'll include a sample calc in the benchmark plan.
[04:38] Priya: about sampling  you mentioned cold vs warm cache. can you describe the measurement plan steps briefly?
[04:44] Diego: yes: 1) baseline single-stream TTFT tests across 1000+ samples, cold start included; 2) warm KV cache tests (after preload) single-stream and small-batch; 3) open-loop ramp tests to measure TPOT and tokens/sec at different target QPS; 4) closed-loop with client pacing to simulate end-user concurrency and backpressure; 5) production replay against staging with real traffic sample; 6) analyze p50/p95/p99 and tail jitter, and snapshot CPU/GPU utilization.
[05:08] Samir: for the replay, do you require traffic obfuscation or can we share raw logs?
[05:12] Maya: obfuscation preferred  removing user-identifying fields is fine; we'll accept anonymized payloads.
[05:17] Priya: billing/commits  if we hit targets in pilot we want a path to reserved capacity. what's the commercial cadence?
[05:23] Maya: we'll include Dedicated/reserved capacity options in pricing we send; typical pilot converts to a reserved commit after successful benchmarks and exec sign-off.
[05:30] Laura: any recommended thresholds for deciding yes/no?
[05:32] Diego: tieback to UX and cost: if TTFT/TPOT within 10-20% of targets and quality within tolerance and cost economics beat your current provider by >15% per token, that's a good signal.
[05:44] Priya: ok that helps. one last question  what about measurement noise and how do you account for it?
[05:49] Diego: we run repeated trials at different times and control for background load; we also instrument tracing for request paths and remove outliers from known noisy infra events. we'll provide the raw logs and processing notebook so you can reproduce the stats.
[06:02] Maya: great. to recap next steps: Maya to send benchmark plan + security docs + pricing; Priya to share traffic histogram and sample logs; Diego to drop microbench scripts and test instructions; schedule follow-up week of Mar 25 to review baseline results.
[06:17] Priya: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[06:20] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up by tomorrow with the plan.
